title: 3D and motion design creators in Australia | MANA
description: 3D and motion design creators in Australia: what green-screen concept films and CGI launch content involve, and what to fix in writing before filming.
h1: 3D and motion design creators in Australia: green-screen concept films, CGI and launch content
lede: A 3D and motion design creator builds the whole concept film in one pair of hands: the idea, the green-screen shoot, the 3D build, the animation and the final composite. In Australia the lane is small, so brands tend to book a named creator with published work rather than brief a studio, and they agree the render, the revisions and the usage window in writing before anything is filmed.

sections.h2: What does a 3D and motion design creator actually do?
body: The output is a short film that could not be shot straight. The creator writes the concept, films the talent and the product against green screen, builds or sources the 3D, animates it, composites the plates together and grades the result. One person holds the idea and the final frame, so there is one person to brief and one person to ask for a change.

MANA represents [Hugo Zbor](/creators/hugo-zbor), a Melbourne creative director and content creator who works this way. His published work includes green-screen concept films for a global footwear brand, a global sportswear brand and a streetwear label, with more than 40 projects shipped and 64K followers on Instagram. The footwear brand booked him twice: one film, then a second.

sections.h2: Why book a creator instead of a studio?
body: Two reasons keep coming up in briefs. The first is format. A concept film for the feed has to read as something a person made and posted, in vertical, with the hook inside the first second. A broadcast edit trimmed to nine by sixteen rarely does that.

The second is scope. Most launch content is one deliverable set, not a production slate, and a creator who shoots, builds and composites their own work can carry it end to end. The trade is that you are buying one point of view rather than a department, so the work you have already seen from that creator is the best guide to what you will get.

sections.h2: What does CGI-led launch content get used for?
body: In practice, four jobs. A product reveal where the product does something physically impossible. A drop or date announcement that needs to feel like an event. A campaign key visual turned into motion for social. And a short loop that can carry paid spend after the organic post.
Green screen is the reason the same creator can do all four. The talent and the product stay real and in frame while the world behind them is replaced, so the product still looks like the product.

sections.h2: What numbers can you ask for before you book?
body: Ask for Instagram insights with a stated window and a date, not a screenshot with no period attached. Ask for non-follower reach, because that is what tells you whether a post travels past the creator's own audience. Ask what was organic and what was boosted.

For a sense of what published roster data looks like: the architecture and design creator on MANA's roster recorded 928K+ monthly views, 40K average reel views and 92% non-follower reach (Instagram insights, 30-day window, June 2026, all organic). One organic reel for a design software brand reached 490K+ views and 29K saves and brought that brand 100+ paid sign-ups, with no boost and no whitelisting. A separate tools reel reached 161K views and 11K saves and drove 25 app sign-ups. Those are reel figures rather than render figures, but they are the test a concept film has to pass: it has to be watched by people who do not follow you, and it has to make someone act.

sections.h2: What should you fix in writing before anything is rendered?
body: A 3D job has more moving parts than a talking-head post, and most disputes are about something nobody wrote down. Settle these before the shoot date is booked. Our longer note on [what to put in writing before anything is filmed](/journal/how-to-brief-a-creator) covers the brief itself.
bullets: Deliverables: how many cuts, what lengths, what aspect ratios, with or without captions and sound.
Revisions: how many rounds, and at which stage each one lands. Changes after the composite is locked cost more than changes to the concept.
Approvals: who signs off, and how long they have. Name one person.
The 3D assets: who keeps the project files, and whether the brand can reuse the build in later work.
Usage: where the film can run, and for how many months from the live date.
Whitelisting and paid: whether the film runs as an ad from the creator's handle, and for how long.
Exclusivity: which category is locked, and until when.
Dates: shoot day, first cut, final cut, live date.

sections.h2: A common way it goes wrong
body: A common way it goes wrong is the usage window. A brand runs the film organically, sees it work, puts media behind it, and the window quietly expires while the ads are still live. Nobody is being difficult; the term was agreed months earlier and then forgotten.

The fix is boring and it is administrative. One contact tracks the dates and raises a renewal before the window closes, rather than after someone notices. That is the part MANA runs: matching, scope, contract and usage, production, approvals and posting, with one person accountable for all of it. If you want to see the work and the audience data first, the overview of how to [work with Australian content creators](/brands) sets out the steps and the media kits.

faq: Are there many 3D and motion design creators in Australia?

No, it is a small lane. Most Australian creators who post 3D and motion work sit inside a broader creative direction practice rather than running a studio. MANA represents one, Hugo Zbor, based in Melbourne, whose published work includes green-screen concept films for a global footwear brand, a global sportswear brand and a streetwear label.
What does a green-screen concept film cost?

We don't publish prices; a film is quoted for your exact scope. The things that move the number are the count of deliverables and cuts, shoot days, how much of the 3D is built from scratch, how many revision rounds you want, how long you need the usage for, whether the film runs as a paid ad from the creator's handle, and whether you want category exclusivity.
Can we run the film as an ad, and do we own the 3D files?

Both are agreed in writing before filming, not assumed afterwards. A first paid post includes three months' usage; longer windows, whitelisting and category exclusivity are separate add-ons quoted with the scope. File ownership and reuse of the 3D build are a line in the agreement, so ask for it to be written down if reuse matters to you.
